about: The Adoro te devote is a Eucharistic hymn that the 1962 Missal prints among the prayers of thanksgiving after Mass and attributes to Saint Thomas Aquinas. In seven strophes of four lines, one worshiper speaks to Christ hidden in the Sacrament. The worshiper adores His hidden Godhead, believes the word of the Son of God where sight, touch, and taste are deceived, confesses both the Godhead and the humanity hidden there, and asks for what the repentant thief asked. Without seeing the wounds that Thomas saw, the worshiper confesses Christ as God and asks to believe Him more and more, to hope in Him, and to love Him. Christ is then addressed as the memorial of the Lord’s death, the living bread, and the loving pelican whose blood cleanses, and the hymn ends with the longing to see Him unveiled and to be blessed by the sight of His glory.

seg.tr: I adore You devoutly, hidden Godhead,
who truly lie hidden beneath these forms.

ex.w011: The verb repeats the hiddenness of “latens” (w004) in a form that stresses lying hidden and remaining so. With “vere” (w010) the line affirms that this presence beneath the visible forms is real, though concealed.

seg.tr: My whole heart submits itself to You,
because in contemplating You it wholly fails.
Sight, touch, and taste are deceived about You,

ex.w028: The passive names no deceiver: sight, touch, and taste are simply mistaken about the One before them. The next line sets hearing alone against all three.

seg.tr: but by hearing alone one safely believes.

nt.w032: “Tuto” is taken as the adverb “safely,” so that the safety belongs to believing. The same form could be the ablative of the adjective “tutus” agreeing with “audítu,” “by safe hearing alone,” which makes the hearing itself safe. Either way, faith that rests on hearing is not deceived.

seg.tr: I believe whatever the Son of God has said.
Nothing is truer than this word of Truth.

ex.w042: Truth is a title of the Son of God named in the line before: in Jn 14:6 He calls Himself the truth. Because this word comes from Truth itself, nothing can be truer.

seg.tr: On the Cross only the Godhead was hidden,
but here the humanity too is hidden at the same time.
Yet, believing and confessing both,

nt.w055: “Ambo” is read as neuter, “both things,” gathering the Godhead and the humanity named in the two lines before. The form could also be masculine, “both persons,” but the hymn names no pair of persons here, and that reading would make two subjects of the one Christ.

seg.tr: I ask for what the repentant thief asked for.

ex.w063: One of the robbers crucified with Christ, who repented and asked to be remembered when Christ came into His kingdom (Lk 23:42). The hymn names that request without repeating its words.

seg.tr: I do not look upon the wounds as Thomas did.

ex.w067: Thomas was shown the wounds of the risen Christ and confessed Him as his Lord and his God (Jn 20:27–28). The speaker does not see them and still confesses Christ as God.

seg.tr: Yet I confess You to be my God.
Make me believe You more and more,
have hope in You, and love You.
O memorial of the Lord’s death,

ex.w088: The Sacrament itself is addressed as the memorial of the Lord’s death, which it keeps in remembrance (compare Lk 22:19 and 1 Cor 11:26).

seg.tr: living bread, granting life to humankind,

nt.w091: “Panis vivus” is read as a title of address in the nominative, standing beside the vocative “memoriále” and calling on the One who is then asked, “Præsta.” Its nominative form, fixed by “vivus,” could also suit a statement such as “You are the living bread,” but the line has no verb and leads into a petition.

seg.tr: grant that my mind may live on You,
and that You may always taste sweet to it.

ex.w107: The verb is used of flavor: Christ is always to taste sweet to the mind. Bodily taste, “gustus” (w025), is deceived in the second strophe, but the mind is to find Him sweet (compare Ps 33:9). The verb can also mean to be wise, an overtone of savoring as knowing that does not replace the taste.

nt.w106: “Dulce” is read as describing how Christ tastes: “te” is the subject of “sápere,” and the prayer asks that He always taste sweet to the mind, “illi.” The words also allow the mind to be the one granted to savor Him sweetly, with “te” as object, like “recta sápere” in the Pentecost collect. In both readings the mind finds Christ sweet to its taste.

seg.tr: Loving pelican, Lord Jesus,

ex.w109: Christ is addressed as the loving pelican, and the following lines show how the hymn uses the image: His blood cleanses, and one drop of it can save the whole world. “Pie” (w108) gives the title its note of devoted, tender love and of holiness.

seg.tr: cleanse me, unclean as I am, with Your blood,
one drop of which, to save
the whole world from all wickedness, has the power.

ex.w124: The verb states what the blood is able to do, not that the whole world is in fact saved: a single drop has power to save the whole world from all wickedness. One drop set against the whole world shows how great that power is.

seg.tr: Jesus, whom I now behold veiled,
I pray that what I thirst for so greatly may come to pass:
that, seeing You with unveiled face,

nt.w143: The Latin does not say whose face is unveiled. Read within the hymn, it is Christ’s, since He is now beheld veiled, “velátum,” and is to be seen unveiled. Paul uses the same words, “reveláta fácie,” of the beholders’ own unveiled faces (2 Cor 3:18), and that reading remains possible. The English “with unveiled face” names no owner and keeps both open.

seg.tr: I may be blessed by the sight of Your glory. Amen.

ex.w144: Sight, “Visus” (w023), is deceived in the second strophe. At the end it returns as the sight of Christ’s glory, through which the speaker asks to be blessed, seeing unveiled the One now beheld veiled (compare 1 Cor 13:12).
